content: Proline-, glutamic acid-, and leucine-rich protein 1 (PELP1), also referred to as the modulator of non-genomic activity of estrogen receptor (MNAR) and transcription factor HMX3, is a protein encoded by the PELP1 gene in humans. It functions as a transcriptional corepressor for nuclear receptors such as glucocorticoid receptors and as a coactivator for estrogen receptors. PELP1 is a transcriptional coregulator that modulates the activity of various hormonal receptors and transcription factors. PELP1 plays critical roles in hormonal signaling, cell cycle progression, and ribosomal biogenesis. Its expression is upregulated in several cancers, and its deregulation contributes to resistance to hormonal therapy and metastasis. Consequently, PELP1 represents a novel therapeutic target for many cancers. PELP1 is expressed in a wide range of tissues, with the highest levels found in the brain, testes, ovaries, and uterus. A shorter isoform of PELP1 is commonly expressed in cancer cells. The PELP1 protein consists of 1130 amino acids and exhibits both cytoplasmic and nuclear localization depending on the tissue. It lacks enzymatic activity and functions as a scaffolding protein. PELP1 contains 10 nuclear receptor-interacting motifs (LXXLL motifs) and acts as a coregulator for several nuclear receptors, including ESR1, ESR2, ERR-alpha, PR, GR, AR, and RXR. It also serves as a coregulator for other transcription factors such as AP1, SP1, NFkB, STAT3, and FHL2. PELP1 has a histone-binding domain and interacts with chromatin-modifying complexes, including CBP/p300, histone deacetylase 2, histones, SUMO2, lysine-specific demethylase 1 (KDM1), PRMT6, and CARM1. Additionally, PELP1 interacts with cell cycle regulators such as pRb, E2F1, and p53. PELP1 is phosphorylated in response to hormonal and growth factor signals, and its phosphorylation status is influenced by cell cycle progression. It is a substrate for cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) and is also phosphorylated by DNA damage-induced kinases such as ATM, ATR, and DNA-PKcs. Functionally, PELP1 acts as a coactivator for several nuclear receptors and regulates genes involved in cell proliferation and cancer progression. It enhances the transcriptional activity of ESR1, ESR2, AR, GR, E2F, and STAT3. PELP1 participates in the activation of ESR1 extranuclear actions by coupling ESR1 with Src kinase, PI3K, STAT3, ILK1, and mTOR. It is involved in E2-mediated cell proliferation and serves as a substrate for CDK4/cyclin D1, CDK2/cyclin E, and CDK2/cyclin A complexes. Studies using transgenic mouse models suggest the existence of an autocrine loop involving the CDK–cyclin D1–PELP1 axis in promoting mammary tumorigenesis. PELP1 has a histone-binding domain and functions as a reader of histone modifications. It interacts with epigenetic modifiers such as HDAC2, KDM1, PRMT6, and CARM1, facilitating the activation of genes involved in proliferation and cancer progression. PELP1 modulates the expression of microRNAs (miRs), and PELP1-mediated epigenetic changes play a significant role in regulating miR expression. Many PELP1-regulated miRs are implicated in promoting metastasis. PELP1 is essential for an optimal DNA damage response, is phosphorylated by DDR kinases, and is critical for p53 coactivation. It also interacts with mutant p53 (MTp53), regulates its recruitment, and alters MTp53 target gene expression. Depletion of PELP1 increases the stability of E2F1. PELP1 binds RNA and participates in RNA splicing. The PELP1-regulated genome includes several uniquely spliced isoforms. Mechanistic studies have shown that PELP1 interaction with the arginine methyltransferase PRMT6 plays a role in RNA splicing. PELP1 is crucial for the synthesis of the 60S ribosomal subunit and ribosomal RNA transcription. The SENP3-associated complex, comprising PELP1, TEX10, and WDR18, is involved in the maturation and nucleolar release of the large ribosomal subunit. SUMO conjugation and deconjugation of PELP1 regulate its dynamic association with the AAA ATPase MDN1, a key factor in pre-60S remodeling. SUMOylation of PELP1 promotes the recruitment of MDN1 to pre-60S particles, while deSUMOylation is required to release both MDN1 and PELP1 from pre-ribosomes. PELP1 is widely expressed in various regions of the brain, including the hippocampus, hypothalamus, and cerebral cortex. It interacts with ESR1, Src, PI3K, and GSK3β in the brain. PELP1 is essential for E2-mediated extranuclear signaling following global cerebral ischemia. It plays a critical role in E2-mediated rapid extranuclear signaling, neuroprotection, and cognitive function in the brain. The ability of E2 to exert anti-inflammatory effects is lost in PELP1 forebrain-specific knockout mice, indicating a key role for PELP1 in E2 anti-inflammatory signaling. PELP1 is a proto-oncogene that provides cancer cells with a distinct growth and survival advantage. It interacts with various enzymes that modulate the cytoskeleton, cell migration, and metastasis. Deregulation of PELP1 in vivo promotes the development of mammary gland hyperplasia and carcinoma. PELP1 is implicated in the progression of breast, endometrial, ovarian, salivary, prostate, lung, pancreatic, and colon neoplasms. PELP1 signaling contributes to resistance to hormonal therapy. Altered localization of PELP1 contributes to tamoxifen resistance through excessive activation of the AKT pathway. Cytoplasmic PELP1 induces signaling pathways that converge on ERRγ to promote cell survival in the presence of tamoxifen. In prostate neoplasms, AR, PELP1, and Src form constitutive complexes in androgen-independent model cells. Cytoplasmic localization of PELP1 upregulates pro-tumorigenic IKKε and secretes inflammatory signals, which, through paracrine macrophage activation, regulate the migratory phenotype associated with breast cancer initiation. Clinically, PELP1 is a proto-oncogene that provides cancer cells with a distinct growth and survival advantage. Overexpression of PELP1 has been reported in many cancers. PELP1 expression is an independent prognostic predictor of shorter breast cancer-specific survival and disease-free intervals. Patients with tumors exhibiting high levels of cytoplasmic PELP1 tend to respond poorly to tamoxifen. However, PELP1-deregulated tumors respond to Src kinase and mTOR inhibitors. Treatment of breast and ovarian cancer xenografts with liposomal PELP1-siRNA-DOPC formulations significantly reduces tumor growth, providing initial proof that PELP1 is a bona fide therapeutic target. Emerging data support a central role for PELP1 and its direct protein-protein interactions in cancer progression. Since PELP1 lacks known enzymatic activity, drugs targeting PELP1 interactions with other proteins may have clinical utility. Recent studies have described an inhibitor (D2) that blocks PELP1 interactions with AR. Additionally, since PELP1 interacts with histone modifications and epigenetic enzymes, drugs targeting epigenetic modifier enzymes may be useful in targeting PELP1-deregulated tumors.
